newsitem.title: UK: Softs outlook - Pressure remains on coffee, sugar.
newsitem.headline: Softs outlook - Pressure remains on coffee, sugar.

text.p: London's coffee and white sugar futures may be exposed to renewed bouts of selling this week while cocoa will struggle to get a facelift on the charts.
January robusta coffee futures, after falling last week, mustered support at $1,415 a tonne, and traders now expect roaster demand to cushion losses.
This contrasts with prospects in New York, where arabica may turn out to be rather feeble.

Sugar players are betting on key support at $300.00 to break, while cocoa has partially reversed its fortunes above a rigid downtrend channel and will try to crack upside resistance. But cocoa bulls may be disappointed. The market saw extensive short covering last week, but the rally was technically inspired and New York crumbled at the sight of a key chart gap on Friday.
CSCE March may have another try at the $1,404-1,408 gap and hunt buy-stops just above it, but the market focus is shifting to fundamentals as Ivorian arrivals enter a critical stage.
November arrivals may point to a harvest just short of last year's record. But some traders say lower output could translate into a big deficit in 1996/97.
Total arrivals of 250,000 tonnes in November would suggest a main crop of about 900,000 tonnes and a total crop of roughly 1.050 million, crop forecasters said.
March cocoa will meet chart resistance at 937 stg a tonne and then at 945 following its unchanged close on Friday at 925.

One trader said, "There are a lot of shorts. If they continue to cover, it's like a snowball. You may get other people to buy because it looks good on the charts." Friday's CFTC report, which showed a decline in speculative longs and an increase in shorts in the two weeks ending November 19, may be seen as bullish but the figures do not reflect last week's short covering.
London will keep an eye on the UK budget on Tuesday to get clues about sterling, but an erratic price trend may set in on Thursday and Friday as New York will be closed for Thanksgiving.
Coffee will seek guidance from New York, where the March contract is close to chart support at 108.40 cents, which may trigger a flood of fund and origin selling.
"If it breaks 108.40 and 106.40 you'll see a sharp drop. That will affect London, but not as much," said one trader.
London's upside potential was also seen limited with $1,475 regarded as key for fund buying. London's January closed $4 down at $1,424 on Friday.
A stream of seasonal coffee is keeping the market under pressure. Ugandan coffee is said to be plentiful, while Vietnamese supplies could gain momentum once the wet spell there abates.
Ivory Coast is expected to reap a higher crop this season.

But under the spotlight is Brazilian coffee estimates for 1997/98. Traders said a report by former USDA analyst Leon Yallouz could take centre stage, possibly this week, as it will be the first independent forecast.
Figures out so far are lower compared with this season because of stress on trees.
Selling pressure may also weigh on white sugar this week.
"I think there's every chance that March can go under $300. I don't see there's anything in the market to stop it unless you can get some really good buying to come out," said one trader.
Narrow to flat spreads would probably deter industry buying, unless prompt demand was acute, as most were already covered.
Quality sugars should remain in abundant supply for the rest of the year at least, and nearby support should be eroded once the few buyers that are around have covered their immediate needs.
"The problem is that those whites buyers will gradually get filled in and so the next time it comes down to around $300 nobody will want to buy it," said one trader.
March sugar closed at $303.20 a tonne on Friday and, below $300, will be looking for support at $298.00 00.
